transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-21 14:30 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Markus Hale (CTO, Copperridge), Lina Ortega (Infra Lead), Evan Brook (Solutions Architect)

Summary:
Quick partner intro between Redwood and Copperridge Systems to scope potential integration: Copperridge is an edge SaaS provider looking to offer GPU-accelerated LLM features to enterprise customers. They want to understand Redwood Dedicated / Private options, network/topology constraints for VPC peering, and a pilot scope for benchmarking throughput & latency.

Topics:
- High-level product fit and partner model
- Deployment options (hosted vs dedicated vs private/VPC)
- Network and security constraints (VPC, egress, KMS)
- Benchmarks and pilot success criteria
- Commercial signals and timeline

Action items (captured live): see metadata field.

Transcript body:
00:00 Jordan Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for carving time. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on the partners team.
00:08 Markus Hale: Hey Jordan, hi Priya, thanks. Markus here, happy to be on. We've got Lina and Evan with me.
00:13 Priya Desai: Hi all, Priya, solutions engineer - I'll dig into the infra and performance bits.
00:18 Lina Ortega: Lina - infra. Quick note, apologies in advance I might jump in with very network-y questions.
00:23 Evan Brook: Evan, I'm a solutions architect. We're exploring how to bundle LLM features into our edge SaaS stack with low latency to our customers.
00:35 Jordan Kim: Love it. Quick agenda: 1) partner model and where Redwood fits in your stack; 2) deployment options and constraints; 3) pilot/benchmark framing; 4) next steps. Sound okay?
00:44 Markus Hale: Yeah, good. We're evaluating a couple of vendors but want to see where Redwood could slot in — especially around dedicated or VPC private options.
00:53 Priya Desai: Great. Markus, can you paint a quick picture of your current infra and what latency/throughput targets look like?
01:02 Markus Hale: Sure. Copperridge is multi-region, but our control plane is in AWS us-west-2. We run customer-facing edge nodes in several colo partners on bare metal. Typical request pattern is spikey — lots of small inference requests, some larger batch jobs for retraining or reranking. Latency targets vary; for the real-time features we want sub-120ms p95 from the edge node to inference response ideally. Throughput — depends: for a given tenant we expect bursts up to a few hundred concurrent small requests.
01:36 Priya Desai: Okay, that helps. A couple clarifying Qs: are your edge nodes able to route to a VPC in us-west-2 for inference, or do we need to consider on-prem/on-colo Private deployments?
01:48 Lina Ortega: Short answer: most of our colos can peer to AWS but we have customers who forbid egress to public cloud, so on-prem options are important. We also have customers asking for customer-managed keys (HSM/KMS).
02:02 Jordan Kim: Makes sense. Redwood has three modes, just to level set: hosted API (fastest), Dedicated reserved capacity (Redwood-managed pools with isolation), and Private (VPC/on-prem with customer-managed control plane). For Copperridge's case it sounds like Dedicated or Private is the fit for enterprise customers who need data residency and KMS.
02:22 Evan Brook: Yeah, and we need to understand the tradeoffs between Dedicated and Private — especially around maintenance, upgrades, and who owns the network egress.
02:32 Priya Desai: Absolutely. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools in our infra with network controls and tenancy separation, but traffic still flows to Redwood-managed endpoints. Private gives you the option to run the control plane in your VPC or on-prem; you can put inference nodes closer to your edge, and use your KMS/HSM. It typically requires more ops on your side, though Redwood automates much of the deployment.
02:56 Markus Hale: How does fallback work? If we run Private and a node goes down, do you fall back to hosted? We want graceful degradation.
03:04 Jordan Kim: Yes - smart routing supports fallbacks. You can set policies for failover to a compatible Hosted or Dedicated model variant. We log fallbacks and surface them in Console for auditing.
03:16 Lina Ortega: Good. Security — we need SOC2 + ISO proof, SAML/SSO, audit logs for every token. Also want to know about encryption in transit and at rest — and if you support customer-managed keys.
03:29 Priya Desai: Redwood supports SOC2 and we have a compliance packet we'll send. For Private we integrate with customer KMS and can use customer-managed keys for model artifacts and logs. TLS 1.2/1.3 in transit, and at-rest encryption for storage and KV caches.
03:47 Evan Brook: When you say KV cache, is that sticky per customer? We want to ensure multi-tenant isolation and not bleed prefixes across tenants.
03:55 Priya Desai: Good point — KV cache is per-deployment and we can shard or namespace caches per tenant. With Dedicated/Private you can have explicit isolation.
04:06 Markus Hale: Let's talk latency — you mentioned model variants. If we pin a model and have a local inference pool in region, what's realistic p95 for a 2k token prompt?
04:17 Priya Desai: For 2k tokens depends on model and quantization. Rough numbers: an optimized Llama-like 7B variant on an A100/RTX class node might be in 100-200ms per token for worst-case — that sounds huge — sorry, I mean per request for short outputs. For longer outputs, it's per token generator latency. We usually benchmark for your workload profile.
04:41 Evan Brook: There's a bit of transcription weirdness — but I get the idea. We'll need a benchmark plan.
04:48 Jordan Kim: We'll propose a benchmark focusing on your common request shapes: small real-time queries (< 256 tokens total), mid-size chats (~512-1024), and some batch reranking. Priya will draft tests capturing p50/p95 and a cost-per-1M-token estimate.
05:05 Priya Desai: I'll include continuous batching and KV-cache hit scenarios — the latter is big for reducing tail latencies and cost.
05:12 Lina Ortega: Network: we have two main constraints: 1) some colos can't open outbound to arbitrary endpoints — they need fixed IPs and firewall allowlists; 2) customers with strict compliance want no public egress — they require us to deploy on-prem in their datacenter.
05:27 Jordan Kim: We can provide static egress IP ranges for Hosted/Dedicated and support VPC peering for Private. For on-prem, we supply an offline installer and ops runbook; it's heavier but doable.
05:39 Markus Hale: Pricing signals? Ballpark for Dedicated or Private pilots? We don't need exact numbers yet but want to know if it's in the same order as other vendors.
05:48 Jordan Kim: High-level: Dedicated is a committed monthly capacity model, pricing depends on GPU class and reserved throughput. Private includes a licensing/platform fee plus infra costs. I'll send a starter SOW/price sheet after the call.
05:59 Evan Brook: Competitors we considered — AetherScale and NebulaCloud — they had different tradeoffs. AetherScale was heavy on on-prem but lacked good batching/cost tooling; NebulaCloud was more hosted-first. Curious where Redwood shines operationally.
06:16 Priya Desai: Our differentiators: unified API across modes, transparent token-level costing in Console, and recommendations for batching/quantization tailored to your workload. Also automatic fallbacks and first-class eval/rollout tooling to avoid quality regressions during model updates.
06:34 Lina Ortega: On rollout tooling — how do you manage model rollouts across a fleet? Canary? A/B?
06:40 Priya Desai: We support canary rollouts, percentage-based traffic splits, and automatic rollback on error rate/latency regressions. You can pin tenants to model versions.
06:50 Markus Hale: For pilot scope — we want to run a test with one enterprise customer who has strict latency and KMS needs. Ideally we prove sub-120ms p95 for their small requests and demonstrate KV-cache hit improvements. Timeline wise, we want a pilot in ~3-4 weeks.
07:05 Jordan Kim: That sounds feasible. Proposed pilot: 2-week benchmarking window, 1 region deployment (us-west-2), use a Private deployment with VPC peering for the enterprise customer — or Dedicated with private peering depending on ops preference. We can align more once we see your network docs.
07:22 Evan Brook: Can we surface telemetry into our observability stack? We need traces, token-level breakdowns, and an event stream for errors.
07:30 Priya Desai: Yes, Console has per-request traces and token breakdowns, and we support exporting logs/metrics to external sinks (CloudWatch/Datadog/Prometheus). For Private, you can ingest directly into your telemetry.
07:41 Lina Ortega: On the KMS front — we need to ensure HSM-backed keywrap for model artifacts. How granular is key usage?
07:49 Priya Desai: With Private we can use your HSM for keys. Model artifacts and logs can be encrypted with your keys. We can provide a security architecture doc; I'll attach it.
07:58 Markus Hale: Great. A quick question on maintenance windows and upgrade windows — some of our customers won't accept downtime.
08:05 Jordan Kim: We do rolling updates and can do zero-downtime upgrades for inference nodes when supported by model format. For control plane changes, we schedule windows but also support emergency rollbacks.
08:17 Evan Brook: Is there any SLA for latency? Or is SLA mostly availability?
08:22 Priya Desai: SLA is primarily availability and throughput for Dedicated; latency SLAs are tricky due to network variability but we can commit to p95 SLOs within certain topologies for Dedicated/Private pilots. We'll capture specifics in the SOW.
08:37 Markus Hale: Okay. Anything else on compliance? We'll need data residency, rights to audit, and contractual language for incident response.
08:45 Jordan Kim: We'll include SOC2 reports, and for Private we'll enable audit logging and grant the right-to-audit clauses in enterprise contracts. I'll route legal to your procurement when you want to see redlines.
08:58 Lina Ortega: One slightly technical ask: our edge nodes use TLS-mutual auth towards backends. Can Redwood support mTLS or client cert auth for inbound requests from our edge fleet?
09:09 Priya Desai: Yes — we support mTLS for authentication for Dedicated/Private endpoints, and we can integrate with your internal CA.
09:17 Evan Brook: Good, that'll help. Another thing — how does model quantization get handled? We have mixed precision needs for some workloads.
09:24 Priya Desai: We supply quantized model variants and can onboard your custom model artifacts. We'll recommend quantization profiles per workload; Redwood Optimize will suggest a profile balancing cost and quality.
09:36 Markus Hale: What are typical on-ramp times? From contract to pilot running?
09:41 Jordan Kim: From signature to pilot often 2-6 weeks depending on network readiness and customer responsiveness. Given you already have peering-capable colos, leaning to the shorter end.
09:52 Lina Ortega: We can target two weeks to share network docs and a PO for a pilot.
09:57 Jordan Kim: Perfect. I'll follow up with a checklist: egress IPs, firewall rules, desired model list, and sample traffic.
10:07 Evan Brook: For the benchmark, include a few test vectors that mimic our real requests — we'll supply a token distribution and sample payloads.
10:14 Priya Desai: Please include worst-case open-ended generation so we can measure tail latencies. Also include cacheable prefixes so we can demonstrate prefix/KV cache benefits.
10:24 Markus Hale: Final quick thing on cost — can you model per-customer cost for a multi-tenant setup if we use Dedicated? We need to show margin to our leadership.
10:33 Jordan Kim: Yes — our Console and reporting give token-level cost and we can produce a cost model for your tenancy breakdown. We'll include rough numbers in the pricing sheet.
10:43 Lina Ortega: Alright, I think that's the main list.
10:46 Jordan Kim: Nice. Recap of live next steps: Jordan to send integration checklist and preliminary SOW/pricing; Priya to draft benchmark plan and propose specific test cases; Copperridge to share network diagrams and sample payloads; set follow-up technical deep dive the week of Oct 27. Any objections?
11:04 Markus Hale: No objections, sounds good. We'll aim to have Lina and Evan supply docs by Friday.
11:10 Evan Brook: One more aside — we've seen weirdness with model metadata and model drift. Do you have a recommended evaluation cadence?
11:18 Priya Desai: We recommend baseline evals before rollouts and periodic golden set runs post-rollout. Redwood Optimize can alert on quality regressions tied to prompt/eval sets.
11:29 Jordan Kim: Okay, we'll close there. Thanks everyone — I'll send the checklist and calendar invite for the technical deep dive.
11:35 Markus Hale: Thanks.
11:37 Lina Ortega: Thanks all.
11:39 Evan Brook: Thanks.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional speaker label overlaps and some speech recognition errors around numeric latency phrasing and per-token/per-request phrasing.
